A litany is a long, repetitive series of things said one after another — usually complaints, problems, requests, or accusations — that feels overwhelming, exhausting, or tedious because of how many there are and how they keep piling up.

Think of it like this: if someone wrongs you and you sit them down and go — "You were late. You forgot my birthday. You never listen. You broke your promise. You embarrassed me in front of my friends. You never apologize..." — and this goes on and on, that is a litany of complaints.
What Separates a "Litany" From Just a "List"

This is the most important distinction to understand.

A list is neutral. It's just items grouped together. A grocery list is a list. A to-do list is a list. There's no emotional weight to it.

A litany, however, carries a sense of:

  • Length — it goes on and on
  • Repetition — the same kind of thing keeps coming, again and again
  • Weight or weariness — it feels heavy, overwhelming, or tiresome to hear

So a litany isn't just "several things." It's a relentless stream of the same type of thing that wears you down as it continues. The word itself contains the feeling of something that just won't stop.
The Connotation (The Feeling the Word Carries)

Litany almost always has a negative or heavy tone. You'll nearly always see it paired with things like:

  • a litany of complaints
  • a litany of problems
  • a litany of failures
  • a litany of grievances
  • a litany of excuses
  • a litany of crimes or charges
  • a litany of errors

You would almost never say "a litany of compliments" or "a litany of achievements" — because the word carries the emotional texture of something burdensome, not something pleasant. Technically it can be used for positive things listed repetitively, but in practice, writers and speakers overwhelmingly reach for this word when the list is grim, frustrating, or exhausting.

The word has a second, more specific meaning in religious settings — and this is actually the original meaning from which the everyday meaning grew.

In certain Christian traditions (such as Catholic, Anglican, and Orthodox services), a litany is a special type of prayer with a call-and-response structure. A priest or leader says a short petition, and the congregation replies with a fixed phrase — over and over, repeating the same response many times.

For example, it might go like this:

  • Leader: "From all evil..."
  • Congregation: "Deliver us, O Lord."
  • Leader: "From all sin..."
  • Congregation: "Deliver us, O Lord."
  • Leader: "From sudden death..."
  • Congregation: "Deliver us, O Lord."

This keeps repeating through many petitions. The congregation's response stays the same; only the leader's part changes. This rhythmic, repetitive, structured prayer is a litany.

You can clearly see how this religious meaning — repetitive, structured, going on and on — gave birth to the everyday meaning. When people started using the word outside of church, they kept its spirit: something said over and over, one after another, in a pattern that feels like it could continue indefinitely.

Here are examples that show the word used naturally so you can feel its weight in context:

  • "After the project failed, the manager sat through a litany of complaints from the entire team."
  • "The inspector found a litany of safety violations in the old building."
  • "She had heard his litany of excuses so many times that she no longer believed a word of it."
  • "The defendant's lawyer was stunned by the litany of charges the prosecution presented."
  • "Every time they met, he would launch into the same litany of everything wrong with his job."

Notice how in every sentence, there's a feeling of "here it comes again" or "this is heavy and relentless." That's the litany.
A Subtle but Important Point: The Role of Repetition

Repetition in a litany doesn't mean the exact same words repeated. It means the same type of thing repeated. In a litany of complaints, each individual complaint may be different — but they are all complaints, coming one after another, stacking up. It's the repeating of the category that creates the litany effect. Like waves hitting a shore — each wave is different, but they keep coming in the same relentless rhythm.

A litany is a long, repetitive stream of the same type of thing — usually negative — said one after another until it feels overwhelming. In everyday language, it describes a seemingly endless list of complaints, problems, accusations, or grievances. In religious language, it is a specific prayer form where a leader and congregation alternate in a structured, repetitive pattern. In both cases, the defining qualities are the same: length, repetition, and a cumulative sense of weight.

When you reach for the word "litany," you are signaling to your reader not just that there were many things, but that those things came relentlessly, one after another, in a way that was exhausting to witness or endure.
